Damage tolerance concepts from metallic structures have been extended to composites but are complicated by the heterogeneous nature of composite damage.
Barely visible impact damage (BVID) is typically defined by a dent depth of about 0.3 mm and impact energies up to 136 J.
Aircraft manufacturers like Boeing and Airbus have standardized BVID definitions and inspection criteria based on dent depth and detectability.
Ply cracks and delaminations are the dominant damage modes in composite laminates after impact.
Delaminations grow under lateral loading due to interlaminar stresses and are influenced by ply stacking sequence and laminate thickness.
Compression after impact (CAI) testing is widely used to assess residual strength but is influenced by test conditions and may not reflect actual structural capacity.
CAI failure involves buckling instabilities and progressive damage growth, making interpretation of results complex.
Nondestructive evaluation (NDE) techniques are essential for detecting BVID and assessing damage severity.
Dent depth does not reliably correlate with the extent of internal damage or residual strength in composites.
Unidirectional composites fail in tension by fiber/matrix debonding and unstable crack growth, and in compression by kink band formation and shear-related failure.
Laminate stacking sequence affects damage patterns and failure progression in composite structures.
Interlaminar fracture toughness at ply interfaces controls delamination growth and damage tolerance.
Residual strength alone is not a sufficient metric for damage severity due to complex damage mechanisms in composites.
Damage mechanics approaches and virtual testing offer promising alternatives for improved damage tolerance assessment.
The FAA Advisory Circular AC 20-107B provides guidelines for damage tolerance and BVID in composite aircraft.
BVID detection probability is around 90% with a 95% confidence interval under standard inspection conditions.
The dent depth after relaxation is considered in defining BVID severity.
Multiple ply cracks can occur within a laminate without immediate catastrophic failure.
Impact-induced damage in composites involves complex interactions between ply cracks and delaminations.
The CAI test standard ASTM D7137 is commonly used for assessing residual strength after impact.
